title: Practice Set PRS4 — Codegen Boundaries
description: Senior applied-architecture track: trace a missing codegen asterisk and recognize when disabling codegen is the correct call. Companion to PSS1.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Senior plan-reading scenarios describe GridUnion Continental at platform scale (850M meters across 4 countries, 30 regions, 6 teams, 8TB+ archive); the CSV itself is a small sample for schema reference.
Substations reference. Anchors cross-team architectural scenarios.

tasks.title: The Asterisk That Disappeared

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team's pipeline used to run in 4 minutes with whole-stage codegen enabled (visible in the plan as the * marker on every operator: *(1) Filter, *(1) Project, *(1) HashAggregate). After a recent refactor that added a Python UDF in a withColumn() call, the pipeline now runs 14 minutes. The architect reads the plan and the * markers have disappeared from the entire pipeline stage. The question: why did codegen break for the WHOLE stage when only one operator added a UDF?
description.task: Why did codegen disappear from operators that don't use the UDF, and what is the architectural fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Previous Runtime: 4 minutes

Current Runtime: 14 minutes (3.5×)

Code Change: added withColumn('risk_score', risk_score_udf(col('exposure'), col('counterparty_id')))

Udf Complexity: PyTorch model inference, 22ms per row

Plan Before Change: all operators have * codegen markers

Plan After Change: no operators have * markers

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan that lost whole-stage codegen markers (*) entirely after a UDF was added in withColumn() upstream of the codegen-eligible chain

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Before refactor (codegen enabled across stage)
+- *(2) HashAggregate(keys=[counterparty_id], functions=[sum(exposure)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(counterparty_id, 800)
      +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[counterparty_id], functions=[partial_sum(exposure)])
         +- *(1) Project [counterparty_id, exposure]
            +- *(1) Filter (exposure > 1000.0)
               +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
                  +- FileScan parquet positions

# After refactor (codegen disappeared)
+- HashAggregate(keys=[counterparty_id], functions=[sum(exposure)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(counterparty_id, 800)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[counterparty_id], functions=[partial_sum(exposure)])
         +- Project [counterparty_id, exposure]
            +- BatchEvalPython [risk_score_udf(exposure, counterparty_id)#88]
               +- Filter (exposure > 1000.0)
                  +- ColumnarToRow
                     +- FileScan parquet positions

fields.label: Why did codegen disappear from operators that don't use the UDF, and what is the architectural fix?
options: The codegen markers are still applied at runtime but no longer printed in .explain() output for plans containing UDFs. Fix: read the Spark UI's stage details to confirm codegen is still enabled despite missing * markers.
The UDF allocation pattern triggered a JIT compilation timeout that disabled codegen cluster-wide for safety. Fix: increase spark.sql.codegen.maxFields to give the JIT more time.
withColumn() always disables codegen because it materializes a new column physically. Fix: use .select() with the UDF expression inline instead of .withColumn(); .select() preserves codegen.

BatchEvalPython is codegen-incompatible; once it appears in the chain, all operators in the same stage lose codegen. Fix: isolate the UDF in its own withColumn() AFTER the heavy chain, so codegen survives upstream.
fields.correctAnswer: BatchEvalPython is codegen-incompatible; once it appears in the chain, all operators in the same stage lose codegen. Fix: isolate the UDF in its own withColumn() AFTER the heavy chain, so codegen survives upstream.
fields.rationale: Whole-stage codegen fuses adjacent operators into a single generated Java method.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats codegen markers as cosmetic; they reflect actual whole-stage fusion.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 5 (Whole-Stage Codegen Internals), PSS2 lesson 6 (Codegen Boundaries and UDFs).

tasks.title: Disabling Codegen Was Correct

description.context: GridUnion's Reporting team's complex case-when chain (200+ branches in a single column expression for tax classification) ran fine in dev but produced JIT compilation timeouts in production. The Reporting senior added spark.sql.codegen.wholeStage=false for that one stage, accepting slightly slower steady-state in exchange for predictable JIT behavior. The architect compares the two plan variants and confirms the right architectural call was made.
description.task: Was disabling codegen the correct architectural call here, and what is the principle?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Case When Branches: 247

Generated Java Method Size: 112KB (over the JVM 64KB single-method limit)

Codegen Enabled Outcome: JIT compilation timeout (8s lookup), then falls back to interpreted; 6.2 min total

Codegen Disabled Outcome: interpreted from start, no JIT thrash; 7.8 min total

Production Workload Runtime Variance With Codegen: high (3-15 min depending on JIT cache)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two plan variants of the same query — one with codegen enabled (huge generated method, JIT timeout) vs one with codegen disabled (slower steady-state, no timeout)

evidence.label: Codegen enabled (default)
evidence.content:
+- *(2) HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[sum(tax)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, 800)
      +- *(1) HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[partial_sum(tax)])
         +- *(1) Project [region, CASE WHEN ... (247 branches) ... AS tax]
            +- *(1) Filter (tax_eligible)
               +- *(1) ColumnarToRow
                  +- FileScan parquet transactions

# Runtime behavior:
#   Generated Java method: 112KB (over 64KB single-method limit)
#   JIT: tries to compile, hits timeout, falls back to interpreted
#   Total: 6.2 min, with 3-15 min variance depending on JIT cache state

evidence.label: Codegen disabled for this stage
evidence.content:
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[sum(tax)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, 800)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[partial_sum(tax)])
         +- Project [region, CASE WHEN ... (247 branches) ... AS tax]
            +- Filter (tax_eligible)
               +- ColumnarToRow
                  +- FileScan parquet transactions

# Runtime behavior:
#   No code generation; interpreted execution from start
#   No JIT activity, no compilation timeout, no cache thrash
#   Total: 7.8 min, with low variance (7.5-8.1 min across runs)

fields.label: Was disabling codegen the correct architectural call here, and what is the principle?
options: Yes — for SLA-critical workloads, predictable runtime beats fastest-case runtime. Codegen-enabled has 1.6 min better steady-state but 9 min worst-case variance; codegen-disabled gives 1.6 min worse steady-state but 0.6 min variance. SLA cares about P99, not P50.

No — disabling codegen is always a regression. The 1.6 min slowdown compounds across runs. Better fix: split the case-when into multiple smaller withColumn() expressions so each generated method stays under 64KB and codegen succeeds.

No — JIT compilation timeouts are environment-specific (the dev environment had different JIT cache state). Better fix: warm up the JIT by running the query 10× during cluster startup so production has the compiled method cached.

Yes, but only as a temporary measure. Long-term: rewrite the case-when as a lookup table joined to the data, eliminating the codegen problem entirely. Disabling codegen masks the underlying complexity.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — for SLA-critical workloads, predictable runtime beats fastest-case runtime. Codegen-enabled has 1.6 min better steady-state but 9 min worst-case variance; codegen-disabled gives 1.6 min worse steady-state but 0.6 min variance. SLA cares about P99, not P50.
fields.rationale: Senior judgment optimizes for tail-latency predictability, not best-case throughput.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats codegen as universally beneficial; for >64KB methods it produces variance.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 6 (Codegen Boundaries), PSS9 lesson 9 (P99 Optimization for SLA-Critical Workloads).
